key_insight: Public brain-tumor MRI benchmarks can look highly accurate even when training and test sets leak duplicate, patient-level, or source-level information.
clinical_relevance: Reported MRI tumor-classification performance on these public datasets may overstate true generalization, so benchmark results should be interpreted cautiously before influencing research or downstream AI development.
method: Audited three widely used public MRI corpora for duplicate, patient, and acquisition-source leakage.
Compared performance across nine architectures and three evaluation conditions.
Used a chest-radiograph negative control to test whether non-anatomical file-header cues could separate classes.
evidence_signal: Leakage was substantial: 28.8% of one corpus’s test split had near-twins in training, another had 22.3% byte-identical test-image leakage, 95.5% of traceable test images shared a patient with training, and header-only features reached 0.959 balanced accuracy.
watch_item: Deduplication alone did not reduce balanced accuracy, so a stable leaderboard does not prove dataset integrity or true model validity.
paper_title: Scores That Hold, Benchmarks That Leak: Measuring Dataset Contamination in Public Brain-Tumor MRI Classification
